title: Foundations of AI
summary: Modern AI is software that learns patterns from data instead of following rules written by programmers. This chapter explains how that learning works, how it led to foundation models and the language models behind chatbots, and why those models still make mistakes that cannot be fully removed. It also covers what scaling can and cannot be expected to deliver, the new vocabulary of 2025 and the state of the debate about artificial general intelligence. Two practical ways of thinking about where AI fits in a business follow, which are cheap prediction and a choice between analytical and generative tools. The chapter ends with one author's experience of writing with AI and for AI readers.

title: Industry and Economics of AI
summary: The AI industry is spending far more on infrastructure than it earns, and the central question is whether that gap will close. This chapter explains the arguments for and against calling the spending a bubble, why vendors price AI below its cost, and how forecasts of AI's economic effect differ. It also covers the concentration of power in a few companies and leaders, the rise of Chinese and sovereign AI, the pressure on software-as-a-service businesses and the new problem of managing the cost of AI inside a company.

title: Strategy and Competitive Advantage
summary: Access to AI does not give a company a lasting advantage, because rivals can use the same tools. This chapter explains where advantage can still come from, how leaders can build an AI strategy step by step, and why executive understanding of AI matters more than technology choices. It also covers the AI factory as an operating model, the structures that let companies scale generative AI and the changing roles of senior leaders. Further sections look at the effect of AI on strategy work and at the reasons partnerships with technology firms so often fail. The chapter closes with how private equity firms build AI capability across the companies they own.

title: Deployment and Adoption
summary: Most companies can start AI projects, but few can move them from pilot to everyday use and show a financial return. This chapter explains how to choose a first project, how organizations mature from experiments to scaled use, and why messy data and weak knowledge systems hold projects back. It also covers how to measure the value and quality of AI work, how people really use generative AI and where it helps or misleads them. Finally, it describes the human and technical obstacles to adoption, including hidden use, low-quality output and technical debt, which is the accumulated cost of software shortcuts.

title: Applications by Function
summary: Generative AI already produces measurable value in a few business functions, and the results differ by function. This chapter walks through software development, customer service, sales, marketing, finance, supply chain and procurement, and research and development. For each one it explains what AI does well today, where human judgment still matters and what slows companies down. The common lesson is that gains come from redesigning the work end to end and not from adding a tool to the existing steps.

title: Organization and Work
summary: AI changes how companies are structured and how people work, because it adds intelligence to a project without adding staff. This chapter explains how hierarchies flatten, how work is redesigned task by task and why the way AI is designed decides whether it helps or displaces workers. It also covers how data and AI leadership roles are evolving, how creativity and human skill are affected, and what the first uses of AI by executives, boards and robots reveal. The main message is that structure and incentives, more than the technology, decide who benefits.

title: The Agentic Enterprise
summary: An AI agent is software that pursues a goal on its own by planning, using tools and adjusting to feedback, instead of only answering questions. This chapter explains what agents are, why most enterprises still see little earnings impact from them and how value appears when processes are rebuilt around agents. It also covers the platform an enterprise needs to run many agents, the shared business meaning that agents need in order to reason correctly and the new market for software that automates work between systems. Finally, it looks at how agents change the contest between startups and established firms, how they change decisions and the new questions they raise for the web.

title: Governance and Risk
summary: AI governance is the set of rules, controls and habits that keep AI systems safe, fair and accountable. This chapter explains how to match the type of control to the kind of AI system, how guardrails and incident plans make generative AI more reliable and why safety depends on the setting in which a model is used and not on the model alone. It also covers audits of algorithmic harm, the risks of treating chatbots as human and the case for choosing the philosophical assumptions behind AI deliberately. It ends with how much independence to give an agent and with Dario Amodei's view of the largest benefits and dangers.

title: Security
summary: AI changes cybersecurity in two ways, because AI agents inside a company become a new kind of trusted insider, and AI models used by attackers find and exploit weaknesses much faster than people can. This chapter explains the new risks that agents add, the controls that can be applied at each phase of deployment and the practical case of a healthcare provider that tested its own agents. It also covers the priorities for enterprise cyber resilience, including accountability before an incident, and how banks are responding to a model that can find thousands of serious flaws in software.

title: Foundations of Cloud Computing
summary: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing resources such as servers, storage and software as a shared, standardized and automated service. This chapter explains the three service layers, which are infrastructure, platform and software as a service, and the ways clouds are deployed, including public, private, hybrid and multicloud. It also covers why most organizations end up with a mix of environments, what makes an application cloud-native, and how standards allow different clouds to work together. A recurring point is that how an application is built matters more than where it runs.

title: Cloud Strategy and Migration
summary: A cloud strategy decides where each workload belongs, what moving it will cost and how it will be migrated. This chapter follows that journey from the unplanned, department-driven start of cloud adoption through a five-stage planning process, the economics of capital versus operating spending and the hidden costs of hybrid environments. It then covers the seven migration strategies, from rehosting to retaining, and the program-level traps that decide whether a transformation succeeds. A recurring finding is that careless lift-and-shift migration often raises costs, while rightsizing and workload-by-workload choices lower them.

title: The Cloud Operating Model
summary: An operating model describes how an IT organization is structured and run to deliver its services. This chapter explains why the older shared-services model, built on hierarchy and rationing, no longer fits the cloud, and walks through Forrester's six layers for designing a replacement, which are customers, value, capabilities, structure, governance and leadership. It also covers the growing role of outside partners, the redesign of application architecture around composability and the shift from a controlling center of excellence to a center of enablement.

title: Operating the Cloud
summary: Running cloud environments well means managing three linked things at once. These are daily operations across hybrid and multicloud estates, the storage and integration of data, and the security and governance duties that come with shared infrastructure. This chapter explains how to manage the different kinds of cloud resources, how to choose service levels, which workloads suit the cloud and how data should be tiered and controlled. It also covers the risks created by sharing infrastructure with other customers and why governance fails unless business and IT own it together.

title: Realizing Value from Cloud
summary: Most cloud transformations capture only a fraction of their potential value, typically plateauing at about 35 percent after five years. This chapter explains that the gap has less to do with technology than with ambition, business engagement and execution skill. It shows where cloud value comes from, why programs stall, what the warning signs and turnaround steps are and how maturity models describe what leading companies do differently, including with AI. The consistent finding is that the companies in the highest maturity states run cloud as a company-wide effort owned jointly by business and technology.

title: Economics of Cloud and SaaS
summary: The cloud changed the economics of the technology industry in three ways. It shifted growth toward a few leading providers, moved financial risk from customers to suppliers and made ongoing use, not the first sale, the source of revenue. This chapter explains how established technology companies that were not built for the cloud can still capture growth, how customers differ in the speed and reasons for adopting cloud, and how a discipline called Consumption Development closes the gap between the value a product could deliver and the value customers realize. It also covers how SaaS companies are judged, including the Rule of 40 and the metrics that investors must read with care.

title: Data as a Strategic Asset
summary: Enterprise data strategy treats data as an asset that must be managed with the same discipline as any other valuable resource. This chapter explains why accountability for a dataset should be separated from ownership, why simply collecting more data is not a strategy and how companies can place a value on data even when accountants do not. It also covers how to start a data strategy small, around the most critical business needs, and how organizations typically progress from scattered efforts to a coordinated program led by senior executives.

title: Data Quality, Meaning and Risk
summary: Data is only useful when it is accurate, understood in the same way by everyone and protected from harm. This chapter explains why most organizations get stuck correcting data errors after the fact, how preventing errors at the source works instead and how HelloFresh made that change. It also covers the questions managers should ask about the data behind an AI model, the shared business meaning that AI agents need in order to reason correctly and the five kinds of data risk that no single executive sees whole.

title: Sharing and Monetizing Data
summary: Companies can earn money from their data by selling it, by building it into products or by combining it with partners' data to improve AI. This chapter explains how to monetize data, starting with existing customers and partners, and how to choose between charging directly and building data into existing offerings. It also covers why marketing should join the enterprise data strategy, how Caterpillar showed what chief executive ownership looks like and how federated learning lets organizations train a shared AI model without handing over raw data.

title: Data Leadership and Roles
summary: Many analytics and AI models never reach production, and a new role, the data product manager, exists to close that gap. This chapter explains what that role does, why the Chief Data Officer role is unstable and why data leadership may dissolve into broader business roles. It also covers how data science is changing from a craft into an industrial discipline, when a dedicated Chief AI Officer helps and when it hurts, and why some organizations combine technology oversight with change management in one transformation role.

title: From Data to Decisions
summary: Data only creates value when it changes a decision. This chapter explains what data mining is, the four kinds of tasks it handles and the standard project process called CRISP-DM. It covers the choices that decide what a learning algorithm can find, how to avoid overfitting, why removing names does not make data anonymous and how business analytics differs from business intelligence. It then shows, through Google's experience, why even a sound model fails to move executives unless it is built around how they decide, using a four-layer framework of data, analytics, decision and narrative.

title: Leading Digital Transformation
summary: Digital transformation succeeds or fails on culture, process and continuous adaptation far more than on the choice of technology. This chapter draws on accounts from six established companies, a four-year Harvard Business School study of more than 8,300 leaders and the earlier Digital Masters research. It explains why building a digitally dexterous workforce is the real goal, why chief executive leadership and people who translate between groups matter, and why the work takes much longer than leaders expect. It also covers the five ways companies reinvent their business models and the Pfizer case, where the obstacle was never the technology itself.

title: APIs and the Unbundling of Industries
summary: An API, or application programming interface, is a contract between a provider and the developers who build on it. This chapter explains why most of the business value of APIs comes from private, internal use, how an API program depends on a chain of five links and what to settle before choosing technology. It then shows how APIs let companies embed specialized outside services directly into their own workflows. That creates specialist providers and orchestrators, new sales channels and ways to earn from idle assets, and it also turns partners into competitors and creates risks that companies must plan for.

title: Platform Business Models
summary: A platform business creates value by letting outside producers and consumers find each other and exchange value, and not by making goods in a linear chain. This chapter explains how a platform is designed around a core interaction, how network effects and learning effects make it hard to copy and how the shape of the network decides how strong that advantage is. It also covers the forces that limit a platform's power, the ethical risks of scale and the way AI shopping agents now threaten the interfaces where platforms earn money. A case study of Instagram shows how a platform's culture and its chosen measure of success shape what it becomes.

title: The Economics of Information Goods
summary: Information goods such as software, films and research reports are expensive to create the first time but almost free to copy. This chapter, based on the book Information Rules by Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian, explains why cost-based pricing fails for such goods, why sellers price by the value to each customer and why buyers cannot judge information before they consume it. It also covers how network effects make growth a strategic necessity, why only two market structures last in the long run, how lock-in and standards battles work and how an incumbent can defend itself against copycats.

title: Customer Centricity
summary: Customer centricity means organizing a company around the lifetime value of its customers and not around the products it sells. This chapter explains why customers differ greatly in value and why firms should invest more in those worth the most. It describes the customer-base audit and the five questions that structure it, the measures of customer lifetime value and customer equity, and the mistakes that undermine decisions based on them. It also covers customer portfolio management, which groups customers by the strength of their relationship with the firm as acquaintances, friends and partners.

title: Designing Products Around Behavior
summary: A successful product has to be usable and also something people return to. This chapter explains two complementary approaches. Nir Eyal's Hook Model describes a four-step cycle of trigger, action, variable reward and investment that turns repeated use into habit. Don Norman's human-centered design makes a product usable in the first place by designing from how people actually behave and think. The chapter also explains feature overshoot, which is the buildup of unused features that makes the useful ones harder to find, and why listening to customer requests alone does not prevent it.

title: Lean Startup and Customer Development
summary: Customer Development and the Lean Startup treat a startup as a temporary organization that is searching for a repeatable, scalable business model, and not as a smaller version of an established company that is carrying out a known plan. This chapter explains the four steps from customer discovery to company building, the pivot as a substantive change to the business model, and early adopters called earlyvangelists who are the right first customers. It also covers the build-measure-learn loop, in which each product version is an experiment, the metrics that suit a startup and growth hacking as a responsibility shared across the company.

title: Marketing Technology and Go-to-Market Strategy
summary: Forrester's research treats marketing technology, known as martech, as a strategic asset and not a tactical purchase. This chapter explains why chief marketing officers should own it personally, what capabilities a stack needs and how an eight-stage cycle keeps investment aligned with business goals. It shows why the stack should be built as a flexible ecosystem of connected parts and not bought as one vendor's suite, and how the market for customer analytics is changing. It ends with the go-to-market strategy that the technology must serve, and a maturity assessment that aligns sales, marketing and product around the audience.

title: Generative AI in Marketing
summary: Marketing teams have moved from excitement about generative AI to the harder work of putting it into production. This chapter explains why AI is not new to marketing technology, how to map any AI capability by its level of autonomy and its technique, and which four prerequisites to meet before adopting it. It describes four groups of marketing executives by maturity and a three-step framework for moving up. It also covers a framework for taking generative AI from experiment to production, which looks at people, process, implementation and measurement.

title: How New Ideas Gain Traction
summary: New ideas often come from outsiders, who are free of a field's habits, yet outsiders struggle to win the backing needed to carry an idea through. This chapter explains why the most creative people tend to straddle the boundary between the familiar and the new, how organizations create that position on purpose and why a single ally can matter more than broad support. It also covers how outsiders can learn insiders' language, how moments of crisis make a system open to ideas it once rejected and why a novel business model succeeds only when it is paired with operational discipline.

title: Building Strategic Innovation Capability
summary: Lasting innovation capability comes from treating innovation as a permanent organizational system and not as an occasional program or a single clever bet. This chapter explains why most companies default to incremental innovation or poorly integrated acquisitions, the eight practices that build a strategic-innovation function and the three competencies it needs. It covers how to scale a proven transformational project inside a mature business and how to use outside innovation ecosystems. It also describes the three traps, which are identity, architecture and collaboration, that derail reinvention even when leaders know the threat.

title: First Principles and the Algorithm
summary: Elon Musk is reported to solve large engineering and manufacturing problems with a five-step process that former Tesla president Jon McNeill calls the Algorithm. The steps are to question every requirement, delete every possible step or part, simplify what remains, speed up the cycle time and then automate. This chapter explains the first-principles thinking behind it, the habit of driving one or two urgent issues relentlessly through recurring reviews and how Musk is applying the approach to Terafab, a planned chip factory. It also records the skepticism of the source, which notes that the same playbook has produced goals that were abandoned.

title: Quality, Manufacturing and the Apple Legacy
summary: A Financial Times investigation traces Apple's manufacturing excellence back through a chain of teachers and students to Homer Sarasohn, an American engineer who taught quality management to Japanese executives in postwar Japan. This chapter follows that chain through Steve Jobs's years at NeXT and Pixar to the process he rebuilt at Apple. It then describes Apple's supply-chain playbook, which drew manufacturing knowledge from suppliers, wrote it into patents and specifications that Apple owned, and used that ownership to bring up competing suppliers. The same approach weakened Japanese manufacturers, but in China it helped build industrial rivals.

title: Creating Corporate Value
summary: McKinsey's four cornerstones of corporate finance explain how a company creates value. Growth and returns on invested capital that exceed the cost of capital create it, only cash flow creates it, share prices reflect market expectations as well as performance, and the value of a business depends on who manages it. This chapter applies the cornerstones to growth strategy, portfolio management, acquisitions, capital structure and communication with investors. It also covers research showing that acquisitions raise combined value by only about 4 percent on average, and that stable companies with almost no revenue growth can still match the market.

title: Strategic Thinking and Prioritization
summary: Strategic thinking is a skill that people develop mainly through informal, self-directed learning. This chapter explains Julia Sloan's finding that effective strategic thinkers move between surfing broadly across many fields and diving deeply into one, and the central insight of game theory that a decision cannot be judged apart from how rivals will respond. It then turns to prioritization, which people and companies do badly, and covers common frameworks such as the Eisenhower matrix, RICE and MoSCoW. It ends with the need to communicate priorities and to stop work deliberately, which most organizations skip.

title: Managing Organizational Bottlenecks
summary: An organizational bottleneck is a point where work stalls. This chapter explains the two kinds, which are task bottlenecks, where one task waits on another, and resource bottlenecks, where the needed resource is not available. It describes the four factors behind them, namely centralization, complexity, fungibility and slack, and a study of 28 large US airlines showing that performance is best when each pair of factors is aligned and not when any one factor is minimized. Southwest Airlines' storm meltdown in 2022 and JetBlue's failure in 2007 illustrate what goes wrong. The chapter ends with a five-step process that managers can follow.

title: Working in Sprints with Scrum
summary: Jeff Sutherland's Scrum is a framework for team-based, iterative work. It replaces the detailed upfront plans of traditional project management with short cycles of delivery and learning. This chapter explains the fixed-length sprint, the three roles, the daily stand-up and the sprint retrospective that closes each cycle. It also covers how teams estimate work in relative points, why velocity is the key measure, the criteria that decide when a user story is ready and done, and why Scrum treats multitasking as a measurable source of waste.

title: High-Performing Teams and Constructive Disagreement
summary: Research on roughly 6,000 people in teams rated as high-performing or average found that a culture of experimentation predicts success better than a concentration of talent. This chapter describes the five habits that keep such teams improving, and why catching problems early separates the best teams most clearly. It then turns to disagreement, which stays constructive because of the words people use more than their private intentions. It explains two gaps that undermine good intentions, five tested ways of speaking that close them and how organizations can train, measure and hire for the skill.

title: Structuring Ideas with the Pyramid Principle
summary: Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle is a method for structuring business writing and thinking. It starts from the observation that the mind automatically arranges information into a pyramid, so a document is easier to read when its ideas are arranged that way in advance. This chapter explains the three rules of a valid pyramid, the SCQA pattern for an introduction, the two ways ideas relate and why a document is best built from the top down. It also covers logic trees and the three modes of reasoning, which help to test thinking when solving analytical problems.

title: Communicating with Presence
summary: Now that AI can write scripts, polish slides and coach delivery, what distinguishes a business communicator is presence, meaning a verifiable human appearing in a widening range of formats. This chapter explains why trust in AI-generated content erodes and why audiences want conversational formats. It describes communication as a system in which one message moves through several formats, the five formats that each need their own mastery and why casual-looking formats are not easier to produce. It ends with what AI cannot do, which is to read a room, and with advice on shaping one's own career narrative.

title: Negotiating in the Enterprise
summary: Skilled negotiators can create leverage even when they have no complete alternative to a deal. This chapter explains how partial alternatives, actions that need no agreement from the other side and a walk-away presented as a warning and not a threat can shift a negotiation. It also shows that dependence between buyer and supplier is usually more balanced than it feels. It then turns to why large companies negotiate poorly for structural reasons, and sets out the recommended fixes. They are to give negotiators no authority to commit, so that they act as problem-solvers, and to replace deal review boards with proactive deal value boards.

title: The Economics of Telecom Regulation
summary: Three economic ideas shaped about a century of US telecommunications regulation, which are network effects, economies of scale and density, and the risk that a monopolist will extend its power into adjacent markets. This chapter, based on the book Digital Crossroads by Jonathan Nuechterlein and Philip Weiser, explains how each idea justified government intervention. It traces the history from rate-of-return regulation before 1996 through the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which gave new entrants the right to connect to incumbents and to lease parts of their networks. It then explains how the internet's layered design shaped the later debates over open access and net neutrality.

title: Restructuring the Telecom Operator
summary: Telecom operators are restructuring both the shape of the business and the way their technology and teams are organized. Vertically integrated operators suffer a conglomerate discount from investors and carry a costly legacy of complexity. This chapter explains the three strategic options, which are separating the network from the services, merging with a rival in the same country and moving toward a utility-like model, each with documented gains and real risks. It also covers three further priorities for chief executives, and at the operating level it shows how business architecture, IT excellence and agile ways of working decide whether operators realize cost and speed benefits and can scale AI.

title: Growth Beyond Connectivity
summary: Core connectivity has become table stakes with slowing growth, so telecom operators are looking for new revenue in consumer ecosystems, enterprise IT services, network APIs, private 5G, sustainability and AI infrastructure. This chapter explains why the old growth engines are exhausted and what operators already earn from adjacent businesses. It shows that business customers are willing to buy beyond connectivity, with security and agentic AI driving demand, but that operators have not yet turned that preference into delivery. It also describes the four ways operators can supply AI infrastructure and the operating model that growth beyond the core requires.

title: Pricing Power and Personalization
summary: Telecom operators are squeezed by slow revenue growth, rising costs and pricing that has become a commodity. This chapter explains two complementary responses. PwC's five Cs of convergence, customer experience, commercial innovation, cost excellence and complexity reduction target pricing power at the strategic level. AI-driven personalization uses the customer, billing and network data that operators already hold to create new revenue through targeted offers, real-time promotions and personalized billing. The chapter also describes the technology stack that personalization needs, and it notes that the sources give no documented deployment and do not address the regulatory and trust risks of using behavioral data.

title: Becoming an AI Operator
summary: Telecom operators are repositioning themselves as AI companies, because efficiency programs and connectivity growth have left the sector behind other industries in shareholder returns. This chapter explains the case for an AI-first reinvention of customer care and network operations, which consultancies estimate could lift earnings by double-digit percentage points, and the four plays that an operator can combine. It covers examples such as SK Telecom, Orange and Singtel and the partnerships with AI-native companies such as Perplexity. It also shows that capturing the value depends less on algorithms than on scaling discipline, which means redesigning workflows end to end and building shared platforms, unified data and early risk involvement.

title: The Technology Foundation for AI-Native Networks
summary: AI-native telecom networks need a different technology foundation from the batch analytics that operators have used for years. This chapter explains the two prerequisites, which are clean multi-vendor data and a cloud-native, programmable network, and the changes needed in computing, networking and storage. It describes teams of specialized agents that act on network, customer and billing data in real time, and the privacy, security, compliance and critical-infrastructure risks that their autonomy creates. It also covers the workload-by-workload choice of where AI runs, with training and sensitive data increasingly kept under operator control, inference at the edge and customer-facing agents in the public cloud with on-premises fallback.

title: Quantum Computing and the Enterprise
summary: Quantum computing is a general-purpose enabling technology whose business value is likely to emerge gradually, through co-invention between vendors and users. This chapter explains why enterprises are better served by early, low-stakes experimentation than by waiting for the technology to look ready. It covers where commercial promise concentrates, which is chemistry and materials simulation, some optimization and fraud detection, and the security risk of Q-Day, the point at which quantum machines can break current public-key encryption. It also reports the early telecom uses, in radio network optimization and quantum-safe networking, and the technical limits and skeptics that temper the enthusiasm.

title: Rich-World Public Debt and Inflation Risk
summary: The Economist argues that the public debt of advanced economies, near 110 percent of GDP and close to an all-time high, has no politically workable path to repayment. This chapter explains why the usual routes are blocked. Spending cuts face the political power of an aging population, immigration only defers the problem, faster growth from AI would not rescue budgets and large tax rises are hard to enact. History shows that large economies have rarely repaid debt from budget surpluses. Of five possible exits from unsustainable debt, the Economist concludes that tax rises, default and inflation remain, and that inflation is the most likely, with holders of long-term bonds the likeliest losers.

title: The US Affordability Debate
summary: The Economist argues that America's affordability crisis is mostly a mirage, because real wages have risen steadily for a decade and are near record highs across income groups, especially for the poorest. This chapter explains why perceptions differ from the data, which is because people focus on price levels and not on rates of change, and because they credit wage gains to their own skill and blame price rises on outside forces. It then covers the real exceptions in housing, mortgage rates and electricity, and the political pressure for price caps. It ends with the Economist's warning that price controls distort markets and tend to become permanent.

title: A Fragmenting Digital Economy
summary: The global digital economy is splitting into diverging national and regional paths, shaped as much by US-China rivalry, regulation and access to AI computing capacity as by markets and technology. This chapter draws on the 2026 Digital Evolution Index, which covers 125 countries. It explains the four groups into which the index sorts countries, why the United States and China dominate digital GDP while pursuing different AI strategies, and why digital regulation is diverging by region. It then shows how Chinese companies, facing trade tensions and tighter scrutiny of foreign investment, expand abroad by targeting microregions, and why Singapore is a favored base.

They cover the exits from unsustainable public debt, the reasons for the gap between data and perception on affordability, the grouping of countries by digital development and the place-based strategies of Chinese companies.

title: Glossary of Economy and Geopolitics Terms
summary: This glossary defines the terms that appear most often in the Economy and Geopolitics part of the Book of Knowledge. Each entry gives a short plain-language definition and points to the Concept where the term is explained in depth. Terms are listed in alphabetical order.
